narrative_md:
**Contract signed 2010. Initial Operating Capability declared 2025. In between: troops hospitalised from the vibrations, a two-year programme pause, and an open question about whether the platform ever earned its £5.5bn.**

Ajax — the British Army's new tracked reconnaissance vehicle family built by General Dynamics Land Systems UK — illustrates almost every failure mode of UK defence procurement. The contract was signed in 2010 for 589 vehicles at £5.5bn. By 2021 the programme was paused over noise and vibration injuring crews. IOC came in mid-2025, 15 years after contract signature and six years later than originally planned.

**The contract.** General Dynamics UK won the Specialist Vehicles (SV) competition in 2010, taking over the existing Scout SV programme. £5.5bn for 589 vehicles in six variants (Ajax reconnaissance, Ares APC, Athena command, Argus engineer recce, Atlas recovery, Apollo repair). The platform was a derivative of the General Dynamics European Land Systems ASCOD, heavily modified for UK requirements — new hull, new 40mm CTAS turret (CTA International, BAE/Nexter joint venture), UK comms, UK electronics. The 'British modifications' on a Spanish baseline became a repeating theme.

**The noise-and-vibration crisis.** From 2018 onwards, trials crews reported hearing loss and joint damage. An MoD-ordered safety pause in November 2020 became a full programme pause in early 2021. Hundreds of soldiers were referred for hearing tests; at least 17 were medically downgraded with suspected long-term injury. The NAO's March 2022 report 'The Equipment Plan 2021 to 2031: The Ajax programme' concluded the programme 'had gone so badly wrong that it was not clear whether it could be brought back on track'. Original IOC date of 2017 was abandoned; 2020 target missed; 2024 and 2025 dates slipped.

**The fix.** Between 2021 and 2024, GDUK re-engineered the suspension, drive-train and engine mountings, added acoustic dampening to the fighting compartment, and modified the ammunition system. Noise levels in the driver position fell from 120+ dB to within safety limits. The MoD and GDUK renegotiated the contract terms including performance milestones. Independent User Validation Trials in 2024-25 confirmed the core platform now met specification for most roles.

**Initial Operating Capability 2025.** IOC was declared for the reconnaissance variant with the Household Cavalry Regiment in July 2025, 15 years after contract signature. Full Operating Capability — all variants across three regiments — is projected for 2028-29. Total delivery by 2030.

**The capital-vs-opex twist.** Ajax is funded through both the Provision of Defence Capability Capital (Fiscal) Additions budget and the Equipment Support line — the platform is so complex it required a parallel support-enterprise contract with GDUK and Babcock. Through-life cost estimates have risen: the 2021 NAO figure of £12.6bn total cost through to 2035 has been updated in MoD accounts to around £15bn. The per-vehicle cost, including support, runs approximately £25m — comparable to or higher than a German Puma IFV.

**The wider MoD problem.** Ajax is one of several major platforms running long-over-budget — Type 26 frigates, AJAX itself, Morpheus, E-7 Wedgetail (reduced from 5 to 3, then back to 5), and until recently the Warrior Capability Sustainment Programme which was cancelled in 2021. The Defence Command Paper 2023 ('Defending Britain in a contested world') and 2024 Strategic Defence Review under John Healey have both committed to procurement reform — single-source contracting rule changes, a new Defence Industrial Strategy, and a National Armaments Director role created in late 2024. Whether the next-generation FCAS, MGCS and Tempest programmes repeat the Ajax pattern is the test. On a 15-year average turnaround, the answer arrives around 2040.
